newsitem.title: UK: Britain starts to warm towards Camilla, 50.
newsitem.headline: Britain starts to warm towards Camilla, 50.

text.p: Camilla Parker Bowles turned 50 on Thursday as Britain grudgingly began to accept the woman who has beguiled Prince Charles for a quarter of a century.

In a poll conducted for the Daily Mirror newspaper, 68 percent of Britons said they were now in favour of the king-in-waiting marrying his long-term lover, a sharp turnaround from public opinion of a year ago.
Camilla was always "the Rottweiler" to Princess Diana -- and much of Britain concurred as the fairytale royal wedding of 1981 turned into an adulterous, ugly breakup.
Now the tide may finally be turning, just as Diana courts bad press of her own.

William Hill bookmakers said it had halved its odds on Charles marrying Camilla after "a flurry of bets", no doubt boosted by the Mirror's mock photographs of Charles and Camilla locked in loving poses.
On Friday, Charles puts a formal stamp on their often covert affair by hosting a lavish party for the woman who is supposed to make the po-faced prince light up, laugh and actually enjoy life.
New Zealand soprano Kiri Te Kanawa, who sang at Charles' wedding, has reportedly been asked to perform again, this time to serenade the real love of his life.

No guest list has been published, nor details announced -- it was supposed to be a private do -- but aerial photographs show a huge marquee had been erected in the sumptuous grounds of Charles' country house.
As for gifts -- past presents between the lovers were said to infuriate Diana -- again there was no word.

"The best birthday present Prince Charles could give to his beloved Camilla today is a gold ring," said the Mirror, even as it admitted no love for the middle-aged divorcee who usurped gorgeous, young Diana.

Yet Camilla's half-hearted acceptance by the public less than a year after his divorce falls far short of an embrace, and any marriage would reawaken doubts about his fitness to take the throne and her right to sit alongside.

The Daily Mail reported that government officials were drawing up guidance for Prime Minister Tony Blair on the constitutional implications of Charles re-marrying. Aides to Blair, however, described the report as "wholly fictitious".
The Mirror simply concluded that Camilla, no icon to women nor sex symbol to men, was no longer an outcast.
"Hatred has been replaced by ambivalence, fury by a shrug of the shoulders. In short, we don't despise her as much as we did," said the Mirror in an editorial.
Charles has known Camilla since 1971 and confessed in 1995 that he had resumed their affair when his marriage broke down. Diana, too, has admitted adultery.
But whereas haughty Charles left the public cold, Diana -- who is all physical strength and emotional weakness -- set it on fire. The older Camilla could not compete, even if she had wanted to.

For like a true royal, earthy, witty Camilla is the model of discretion. She has never spoken to the press and has never willingly been photographed. Even her former husband says nice things about Camilla in public, despite the fact he was Britain's best-known cuckold.
Yet just as Camilla seems to be rising in the public's esteem, her one-time rival is falling as story after story questions Diana's common sense.
This week, Diana tantalised Britain with the promise of a big surprise announcement about her future -- only to backtrack on her bombshell with a terse statement.
She also admonished the press for trailing her on a private holiday in very public St Tropez, where she was repeatedly spotted in controversial company and a leopard-skin swimsuit.
Even allies urged Diana to see sense.

"Your friends and fans see a woman who is drifting on the sea of life, seriously in danger of becoming shipwrecked," wrote one-time confidant Andrew Morton in the Sun. "To say they are disappointed by the sight of you cavorting around St Tropez like an aspiring starlet from a B movie is an understatement."
